questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Notice that for each vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
${e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}].$

Since ${e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ 

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y={{field-3}}
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form

Since ${e}^{3t}\to $

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}2t-1 \\ 2t\end{aligned}].$

{\begin{aligned}x=4(2t-1){e}^{3t} \\ y={{field-6}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =3,\,v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]t{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}2t-1 \\ 2t\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/c993f6fc9eb12c0d8f60c420519a7db4a5cf78da9f0c24d0ade87b0a96590f59.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}2t-1 \\ 2t\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=4,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=4(2t-1){e}^{3t} \\ y=8t{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-1.79$ | $-4$ | $-4.37$ |
| $y$ | $-0.89$ | $0$ | $2.92$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/6cc714f7f703eaebf31983882cbe988742ea47a9e280c7fbee1f44c877952b63.png)

The matrix of our system is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that:

- Since the only (repeated) eigenvalue of $A$ is positive, we have a $\text{unstable}$ node.

- Since $A$ is not diagonal and has a repeated eigenvalue, there is only one linearly independent eigenvector. So, we have a $\text{degenerate}$ node.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Phase Portrait of a System With Repeated Eigenvalues
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector $\mathbf{v} = [1, \ -1]^T$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $\mathbf{w} = [0, \ 1]^T$ is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ Sketch the phase portrait of the linear system above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/15e5c3f06172ad8218375d20178b96a80de122300761fa4a615aca099d13c52a.png) 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ -t+1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/daa87299ff267ce47cf44b06b218f533de30e780b12905d0e0a1888a50893dd0.png) has the equation 

$$
y= -x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/869e6bf67c0a5826b8d29130e8bf2107674508a103c4fb5a3d7d70ab78577090.png)
lie on that line. 

Since $e^{-2t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/523dccf73169d02b6bdf4297e96ec84bcc6c43213cdd722000f3a987a534b218.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/4fc6300682b6e28d47e43802aba9427e29c606fc6c4f77edad874e7c0e4e2c01.png)
When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{-2t} \\ y=(-t+1){e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-1.36$ | $0$ | $0.18$ |
| $y$ | $4.08$ | $1$ | $0.18$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/dbf5a13ecd5e81c399204fd29d235e410fcb62274555cf3e5b32a383c1078d24.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/6c84cd04f3b037bee48d02d3183114e2668fbbd110bd44e9311e7ff454db8bac.png)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Classifying Systems of Linear Differential Equations With Repeated Eigenvalues
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above, where the system's matrix has repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=5$ of multiplicity two. Determine the type and stability of the equilibrium point for this linear system.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The matrix of our system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/7d16f04f098fc32370423b1b7adaa84c14b92291bde82672b65977b0498ec011.png)

Notice that:

- Since the only (repeated) eigenvalue of $A$ is positive, we have a unstable node.

- Since $A$ is not diagonal and has a repeated eigenvalue, there is only one linearly independent eigenvector. So, we have a degenerate node.

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:
